records.title: Show HN: I wrote an entire Vim manual over 4 years
records.author: thanato0s
records.storyText:
I'm glad to announce that I'm releasing my new book, Learning to Play Vim.

When I started using Vim more than a decade ago, I wished there was a manual out there teaching how to use this fantastic editor step by step, beginning with the foundations up to more advanced features. Of course at the time I did the vimtutor, but it was too dense for me to remember much from it. I also read the entire Vim manual (`:help manual`), but I didn't like it: it was too detailed in places (for example `02.8 Finding help` completely lost me for a while), and other features didn't get the treatment they deserved.

So I decided to write my own Vim manual. It took me more than 4 years and 2987 focused pomodoros (1244 hours) of work to finally get it done!

The result:

- 21 chapters showing the most important Vim features step by step.

- 170 exercises with solutions.

- Many real-life examples to show how Vim can be used and configured for your own needs.

- The related Vim's help pages to dig further into each feature.

Most configs are both written in Vimscript and Lua for Neovim users. This book explores the common features between Vim and Neovim, so don't expect anything about Neovim-specific features (like treesitter or LSP for example).

- The landing page: https://themouseless.dev/vim/

- A sample of the book with the entire table of contents and the first three chapters covering most of the basics: https://themouseless.dev/content/learning_to_play_vim_sample....

I wrote this with my bare hands, no LLM involved to spoil the fun.

records.title: Show HN: Hozo compiles React Native to native UI and semantic HTML
records.author: tanao
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

I've worked with React Native for years, but I've never been fully satisfied with it. That's why I'm building Hozo, an open-source UI compiler written in Rust.

In short, Hozo is yet another cross-platform UI framework like React Native Web, Tamagui, React Strict DOM, and Lynx.

The idea is to share source code, not necessarily runtime abstractions. For example, a Heading compiles to an h2 on the web and a Text with the header role on iOS and Android.

* Web: Semantic HTML and CSS without react-native-web.

* Mobile: Standard React Native components and precomputed StyleSheets.

* Styling: Tailwind CSS and StyleX with CSS-like text inheritance on React Native.

* A11y: First-class support with platform-specific semantics and compile-time ARIA validation.

* Guardrails: Compile-time diagnostics for both humans and AI agents.

Hozo supports SVG, 2D Canvas, Three.js, and WebView. It works with Vite, Next.js, Astro (including zero-JS static components), Metro/Expo, TanStack Start, Tauri, and Storybook. There's also a component library with an optional shadcn mode, and migration tooling for existing RN projects.

It's still early, though. I'm curious what others think of Hozo.

Docs: https://iray-tno.github.io/hozo/docs/

records.title: Show HN: Fmgrep – indexed grep over a persistent FM index
records.author: pepeiborra
records.storyText:
fmgrep is a (Claude-powered) open source reimplementation of a FAANG code search engine I was involved in a few years back. It's aimed at very large (e.g. AOSP) source trees.

Back then we wanted to get our hands on the Github search engine (https://github.com/danlark1/sparse_ngrams) but it was not available, so we went a different way.

Instead of n-grams,`fmgrep` builds an FM index of the tree with O(pattern) `count` and O(occurrences) `locate`, which is quite cool and leads to blazing fast performance as seen in the benchmarks.

records.title: Show HN: Evalkit for Improving Your Agents
records.author: adityamehta1990
records.storyText:
I wanted to share evalkit - an open source framework for improving agents that we built.

https://evalkit.inferedge.com/

Like most people, we used phoenix, langfuse, but these are good recording traces, managing datasets etc. But the process around evals, agent improvements, regressions, mapping errors/failures to code or prompts has to be hand rolled. We still use self-hosted phoenix, but mainly as a database.

Our process was trace mining, converting them into evals, getting them reviewed by an expert, and then re-running datasets to create baseline scores or internal benchmarks for our agents.

We found other companies also follow similar processes in-house, but there is no good framework to do everything e2e. So we carved out what we built into evalkit.

- evalkit automatically groups similar traces into one issue bucket (similar to how one issue in sentry can link to multiple events) - Expert review workflow with simple english rubrics (instead of json) - Coding agent first approach - we expect your coding agent to be able to do most steps, and you rarely have to open the UI

An example of how we used it in-house: evalkit identified 89 traces in on bucket, suggested 14 cases, which resulted in 4 merged PRs. We saw 90% reduction in failures, 80% reduction in token consumption (and cost), and 45% in time.

This is pretty early, and we are adding features every few days. If you feel this is useful, or have any suggestions, reach out to us on evalkit@inferedge.com or join our slack community and give us some love by starring us on github :)

Anytype comes to mind as a similar app but there are some key differences - Hubris feels like an online app despite being decentralised, with live cursors, and real-time edits just like Figma or Google Docs, and it is a one time purchase. I may have subscriptions in the future for people who want integrations with centralised apps and cloud convenience but you can use Hubris fully without it. And since devices sync directly with each other there are no file size or transfer limits.

It's a native Rust app out on desktop right now and it's coming to mobile in the near future. Something to look forward to is third-party plugin support! Everything you see in the app is already a plugin, but soon you can make your own plugins/apps in Hubris while I handle accounts, sync, storage for you - basically allowing you to make online apps that are fully private and decentralised without the infra cost centralised apps come with

I want Hubris to be an option for people to get out of big tech and empower the common user to have inherent privacy and an intuitive user experience while all the complicated decentralised stuff is handled for you. Would love to know what people look for in a product like this and how you would want to use it in your own life/people you work with

records.title: Show HN: Slate, a C to Rust Transpiler for multiple targets
records.author: idobe
records.storyText:
Hey HN, For the past half year I've been working on Slate, my C to Rust transpiler. Slate parses C code as gcc/clang/msvc would, and then translates code to rust. The best supported "flavor" as I call them is clang, with clang flavor I've been able to translate the Linux kernel (built for x86_64 defconfig) and booted the built vmlinux to a busybox shell. Code is here: https://github.com/takashiidobe/slate-linux. Same for projects like Cpython: https://github.com/takashiidobe/slate-python, and SQLite: https://github.com/takashiidobe/slate-sqlite. For an example of a multi-target build, I translated zlib to all targets slate supports with 9 features: https://github.com/takashiidobe/slate-zlib.

Since the entire stack is written in Rust, I compiled to wasm and have a fully client side compiler-explorer esque demo as well: https://slate.takashiidobe.com/.

I wanted slate to be easy to use, and also emit code that a dev would want to maintain. It's one binary (cargo +nightly install slate-c2rust --locked), and comes with a subcommand to set up sysroots (for cross-target builds). Instead of supporting only the clang ecosystem (as many existing transpilers do), I wrote my own C parser stack so I can emulate the three major C compilers for multiple targets, and do things like keep comments, do rewrites based on where functions/macros/definitions come from with header tracking, and also handle flags differently based on compiler. There are currently a couple dozen rewrites, like removing muts, lifting pointers to higher level types, solving gotos, improving inline asm, etc,

Slate aims to support all of modern C, including compiler extensions, like all builtins, intrinsics, inline asm for the three major compilers, and flags. Target support (for now) for x86_64, aarch64, i686, arm32, on linux, windows, mac. Of course this is a gargantuan task but I'm chipping away little by little.

Regressions and testing are a big deal for me trying to scale up the project. I have thousands of tests that run per commit, and do oracle and snapshot testing (with filecheck), so every rust binary translated has to have the same exit code as the oracle (C translated by clang, gcc, msvc w/ wine). That gives me confidence that I'm neither worsening codegen nor breaking any past code as I add new functionality. At this point I have over a million lines of tests, and I'm trying to catch more cases day by day.

Hope you try it out!

records.title: Show HN: Talira – Search engine for software, built for AI agents
records.author: nathan_f77
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Nathan. I wanted to share a project that I've been working on this month.

A few weeks ago, my Rust target folders had grown to about 70 GB across many git worktrees, and I asked Claude to figure out how to stop that from happening. It couldn't find much online, so we started to build our own workaround using some unstable cargo flags. Then someone on r/rust asked why we hadn't just used kache. Someone else mentioned Mr Boxington on a GitHub issue (another great solution).

I also got annoyed that my Claude Code sessions would constantly ask me to reauthenticate my MCP servers, which happens when you run a lot of them in parallel. An agent couldn't find any good "MCP proxy" so we started planning and building our own. I searched Google myself and found MCPProxy.app. It worked pretty well so I wrote a blog post and shared it on X. Some people replied and told me that Executor.sh was an even better solution. They were right, so I switched to Executor.

After all this, I decided to build Talira: A search engine for software that an AI agent can check before it starts building your own solution. You describe the problem in plain words ("my Rust target folders use 80 GB across git worktrees"). Talira searches the catalog using vector embeddings and uses Jev for filtering and reranking.

To try it:

- Search on https://talira.ai

- Add the MCP server to Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http --scope user talira https://mcp.talira.ai/mcp

Your agent can also send a report after each search: the problem in general terms, what you tried, what you kept and why. The idea is that it can eventually become a crowd-sourced database of tools that people actually chose and continued using over time.

It's currently in beta and the catalog still has a lot of gaps. I should also mention that I'm aware that ChatGPT and Claude already know a lot and are already very good at search. So there are plenty of cases where you don't need Talira at all. I'll need to collect some more real-world searches before I can benchmark it properly to see if it makes any difference.

I'd like to know if you've ever had any similar experiences. Let me know if an AI wasn't able to find a good solution that already existed.

Thanks for reading!

records.title: Show HN: HeyCube – The personalized feed for your always-on AI agents
records.author: fengli_wu
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Fengli, founder of Inxpanse. HeyCube is our first product: the personalized feed for your always-on AI agents.

While building my own always-on agents, I kept watching the token and search API costs add up really fast. Then I noticed the scheduled tasks in ChatGPT/Grok Bot/etc. also use up a lot of your plan's allowance, often on checks that find nothing new. That's why many people still don't leave their agents truly always on.

This reminded me of the eras we humans have been through too: first search engines, then feeds. So I thought, why not build agents a feed of their own? That's why we built HeyCube. It reads sources around the clock and sends what fits you to the right agent, so your tokens go to the work itself. It's free and live at heycube.ai now, and works with ChatGPT, Grok Bot, Muse, Claude Code, and other agents in beta.

I'm looking forward to you giving your agents a feed and seeing what they can do. Let me know if you have any questions/comments/feature requests :) Thanks!

records.title: Show HN: Dualayer Hierarchy Standard (DHS) – Zero-FHS Layout for Musl and Glibc
records.author: defaultx404
records.storyText:
Dualayer Hierarchy Standard (DHS:

Repo: https://github.com/Zainium-Dynamics/dualayer-hierarchy-stand... Full Specification (23-page PDF): https://zainiumdynamics.tech/dhs

DHS 1.1 defines a layered filesystem hierarchy for immutable Linux systems where musl and glibc coexist side by side without conflict. Either C library can be primary; the distribution chooses.

Root layout (no /usr, /bin, /sbin, /lib, /lib64, /etc, /var, or /boot at /, not even as symlinks):

  /
  |-- overlayer/   (the entire OS: all layers)
  |-- home/        (user home directories)
  |-- root/        (root home)
  |-- dev/         (devtmpfs)
  |-- proc/        (procfs)
  |-- sys/         (sysfs)
  |-- run/         (tmpfs; removable media at /run/media/user/label)
  `-- tmp/         (temporary files)
Layer structure under /overlayer (composed at boot via OverlayFS with syshub as lower and userland/union as upper):

  /overlayer/
  |-- syshub/           (read-only base OS; boots without userland)
  |-- userland/         (installed packages: union/, work/, registry/)
  |-- ignition/         (kernels, initramfs, bootloader; read-only)
  |-- agents/           (optional AI coding agent instructions/policies)
  `-- .syshub-pending/  (staged atomic base upgrade, applied at next boot)
Dual-libc isolation: musl and glibc each live in their own GNU target-triplet directory (arch-vendor-linux-musl and arch-vendor-linux-gnu) with separate loaders, headers, C++ runtimes, loader configs, and toolchains. Shared directories (/overlayer/syshub/bin, lib, include) belong strictly to the primary libc and search paths never cross, while both read shared system config (passwd, hosts, resolv.conf, zoneinfo) from /overlayer/syshub/etc.

FHS compatibility: Foreign packages are adapted at install time (PT_INTERP, RPATH, pkg-config, shebangs). Runtime FHS path lookups use a preload resolver and loader redirection (the known LD_PRELOAD limitation for static/setuid binaries is documented in Chapter 7).

Reference implementation — Zainium OS (https://github.com/Zainium-Dynamics): - Layers: syshub (base), zexlib (userland), zaisys (ignition) - Libc design: Design A (musl primary in base, glibc as a userland package) - Boot & atomic upgrades: quantra-ramfs - Package manager & receipts: zex - Path/loader resolver & toolchain switcher: libsys_resolver.so, sys-resolver - Protected base/ignition paths: elevate, elevate-pam

Looking for honest technical critique on where this layout holds up, where it breaks down, and what edge cases are missing.

records.title: Show HN: Gpython – A Terminal based notebook for Python
records.author: theredcap
records.storyText:
I was fed up with IPython and the default Python, editing more than one line is painful. But Jupyter and marimo both need a server and a browser tab just to try an idea. I wanted a notebook that opens like a vim does

So I built gpython. It is a notebook in the terminal, built on Textual. Cells are reactive like marimo and has vim keys. You can open both ipynb and .py files like marimo supports. It also has image support for supported terminals and is the fastest among marimo and jupyter based on our limited benchmark test.

Try it without installing: uvx --from gpynb gpython

It is early (0.2.3). I would love feedback on it's usability. And I am curious: would you use this in place of IPython or Jupyter for quick work? If not, what is missing?

records.title: Show HN: Pintura – YAML Slides for agents to edit and humans to review
records.author: danielochoa0620
records.storyText:
Pintura is designed for AI agents to work on plaintext files and for humans to review in a browser.

The premise is that when you're doing slides with AI agents, you mainly need to review their work and iterate until you're happy.

The main benefits are: 1. You can use git for version control and clear diffs. 2. The browser UI is designed for review: flip between versions with visual changes highlighted, pin comments, or drag/reword directly. 3. Your agent gets a CLI that helps it catch things like text overflow, misaligned elements, hanging words, etc.

It pairs with our spreadsheet companion Libreta (github.com/editide/libreta) if you want to link numbers. Clicking a linked number on a slide pops up a spreadsheet showing the formula or a screenshot of the original source.

I've been using this to build financial decks from the terminal with Claude Code (and now Antigravity). It's much nicer than flipping back and forth between Excel and PowerPoint. Here are some decks I've built with this setup: https://iterativaresearch.com/

Everything (preview, checks, screenshots, HTML/PDF export) is Apache-2.0 and runs locally with no account. PowerPoint export currently runs through our API with a free plan.
